lessons.title: Nutrients in our food
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can't we live on just one food, even a healthy one?
objectives: Name the seven components of a balanced diet
Identify foods rich in each nutrient
Explain why we need a variety of foods
successCriteria: List the seven components of a diet
Give two food sources for each
Explain why no single food provides everything
lessons.crossCurricular: Food technology: menus; Islamic Studies: eating halal and tayyib (good and wholesome) food
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude for food (saying bismillah and alhamdulillah); moral: food waste

keywords.def: a substance in food that the body needs
a nutrient that gives energy, e.g. starch and sugar
a nutrient for growth and repair
fats and oils: store energy and insulate
eating the right amounts of all the nutrients

starter: Bismillah. What did you eat for breakfast?
Name a food that gives you energy

teach.heading: Seven components
teach.note: Ask pupils to sort their breakfast into components.

head: Component
Main use
Good sources
rows: e.g. calcium for bones, iron for blood
keeps food moving through the gut

teach.heading: No perfect single food
bullets: Rice: lots of carbohydrate, little protein
Milk: protein and calcium, little iron or fibre
teach.note: Answer the big question with these examples.

teach.heading: Fibre and water are components too

misconception.wrong: Fibre is useless because we can't digest it
misconception.right: Fibre helps food move through the gut and prevents constipation

check.q: Which nutrient is mainly for growth and repair?
check.why: Proteins build and repair tissues. Carbohydrates and lipids are mainly for energy.

practice: Which nutrient is in olive oil?
Give two foods rich in protein
independent: Core: Analyse a meal (rice, daal, salad, yoghurt): list the nutrients each food provides
Extend: Design a balanced iftar menu and justify each choice by nutrient
Stretch: Explain why a vegetarian diet needs careful planning to get enough protein and iron, with examples.
exit: What does fibre do?
Name a food rich in carbohydrate.

lessons.homework: Keep a one-day food diary and label each food with its main nutrients.
lessons.send: Support: food picture cards. Stretch: nutrition labels.

lessons.title: Food tests
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we prove what is inside a food without a label?
objectives: Describe tests for starch, sugar, protein and fat
Interpret positive and negative results
Use results to identify nutrients in unknown foods
successCriteria: Name the reagent and positive result for each test
Interpret results tables
Plan safe, fair food tests
lessons.crossCurricular: Food technology: food analysis; Maths: recording results

keywords.def: a chemical used in a test
turns blue-black with starch
turns from blue to brick red when heated with sugar
turns purple with protein
shows the substance is present

starter: Name the seven components of a diet
Name a safety rule in a lab

teach.heading: The four tests
bullets: Each nutrient has its own test
teach.note: Show the teacher demonstration video of each test with clear before/after colours.

teach.heading: Interpreting a results table
bullets: Match each colour to a nutrient

model.problem: Food X: iodine stays orange; Benedict's turns brick red; biuret stays blue. What does X contain?
steps: Iodine orange: no starch
Benedict's brick red: lots of sugar
Biuret blue: no protein
model.answer: X contains sugar only (e.g. glucose drink)

misconception.wrong: Iodine turns orange when starch is present
misconception.right: Iodine turns blue-black with starch; it stays orange-brown without

teach.heading: Safety
bullets: Ethanol is flammable: no flames nearby
Use a water bath to heat Benedict's
teach.note: Online lessons: watch demos; home versions only for iodine on potato (with an adult, iodine from a pharmacy is an irritant).

check.q: Biuret solution turns purple. What is present?
check.why: Biuret detects protein. Iodine detects starch; Benedict's detects sugar.

practice: What colour shows lots of sugar?
independent: Core: Interpret a results table for five foods and say which nutrients each contains
Extend: Plan how to test a sandwich for starch, protein and fat, with safety precautions
Stretch: Benedict's gives green for one drink and brick red for another. What does this tell you, and how could you make the comparison fair?
exit: Reagent and positive result for starch?
Why heat Benedict's in a water bath not a flame?
What does a purple biuret result mean?
lessons.homework: Draw a results table for testing milk, bread, apple and peanuts, predicting each result with reasons.
lessons.send: Support: colour cards for each test. Stretch: semi-quantitative Benedict's test.

lessons.title: Energy in food
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a builder need more food than an office worker?

keywords.def: unit of energy; 1 kJ = 1000 J
another energy unit used on labels; 1 kcal ≈ 4.2 kJ
how much energy a person needs each day
all the chemical reactions in the body

starter: What unit is energy measured in?

teach.heading: Energy from food
bullets: Carbohydrates and lipids are main energy sources
Lipids store more energy per gram
teach.note: Show labels: oats about 1600 kJ/100 g; butter about 3000 kJ/100 g; apple about 220 kJ/100 g.

model.problem: Cereal has 1500 kJ per 100 g. How much energy is in a 40 g bowl?

teach.heading: Different people, different needs
bullets: Age and growth: teenagers need a lot

misconception.right: Proteins do release energy, but the body mainly uses them for growth and repair

check.q: Biscuits: 2000 kJ per 100 g. Energy in 25 g?
check.why: 2000 ÷ 100 × 25 = 500. A multiplies by 4 instead of dividing; D adds.

practice: Which has more energy per gram: fat or carbohydrate?
Bread 1000 kJ/100 g: energy in 60 g?
Why does a teenager need lots of energy?

Energy in 50 g of a food with 400 kJ/100 g?
Give two factors affecting energy needs.
lessons.homework: Collect three food labels and calculate the energy in your usual portion of each.
lessons.send: Support: calculation frame. Stretch: kcal to kJ conversions.

an illness caused by lacking a nutrient
having so much body fat it harms health
eating too little food for a long time

starter: Energy in 30 g of food with 1200 kJ/100 g?
Which mineral is needed for strong bones?
Name a source of vitamin C

teach.heading: Malnutrition
teach.note: Answer the big question: someone eating mostly fried snacks can be overweight but lack vitamins and minerals.

teach.heading: Deficiency diseases
bullets: Each missing nutrient causes particular symptoms

teach.heading: Getting more vitamin D
bullets: Made in the skin with sunlight
Also in oily fish and eggs
teach.note: UK guidance: consider a vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. Links to people who cover their skin or live indoors.

misconception.right: Malnutrition means an unbalanced diet, which can cause obesity

check.why: Rickets is caused by too little vitamin D (or calcium). Vitamin C causes scurvy; iron causes anaemia.

lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the design of the body; sunnah of eating with the right hand and not overfilling the stomach (hadith in Sunan Ibn Majah: a third for food, a third for drink, a third for air)

keywords.def: breaking large food molecules into small soluble ones
tube carrying food from mouth to stomach
where most digestion finishes and food is absorbed
where water is absorbed
where faeces are stored before leaving the body

starter: Name the organ that pumps blood

teach.heading: The journey of food
teach.note: Answer the big question with the timeline.

timeline.label: Mouth
timeline.text: teeth chew; saliva starts starch digestion

timeline.label: Stomach
timeline.text: acid and enzymes digest protein; churns

teach.heading: Why digest?
bullets: Starch, protein and fat molecules are too big
They must pass into the blood
teach.note: Use a model: a 'visking tubing' gut (video). Starch stays in; glucose passes through.

teach.heading: Helper organs
bullets: Food does not pass through them

misconception.wrong: Food passes through the liver and pancreas
misconception.right: They add bile and enzymes; food stays in the gut tube

check.why: The large intestine absorbs water. The small intestine absorbs most digested nutrients.

practice: Put in order: stomach, mouth, small intestine, oesophagus
independent: Core: Write a 'journey of a date' story, naming each organ and its job
Extend: Explain why food molecules must be small and soluble to be absorbed
Stretch: Explain the sunnah guidance on filling the stomach a third with food, a third with drink and a third with air, in terms of digestion.

What does the large intestine absorb?
Why must food be digested?

lessons.title: Enzymes in digestion
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does bread taste sweeter the longer you chew it?
objectives: Describe enzymes as biological catalysts
Match digestive enzymes to their food molecules and products
Explain the effect of temperature and pH on enzymes
successCriteria: Name amylase, protease and lipase and what they digest
State the products of each enzyme
Explain why enzymes work best at certain conditions
lessons.crossCurricular: Food technology: enzymes in cheese and baking; Chemistry: catalysts
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the precision of biological systems

keywords.def: a protein that speeds up reactions in living things
speeds up a reaction without being used up
enzyme that digests starch into sugars
enzyme that digests proteins into amino acids
enzyme that digests lipids into fatty acids and glycerol

starter: Name the organ that makes bile

teach.heading: Three enzymes
bullets: Each enzyme digests one type of molecule
teach.note: Answer the big question: amylase in saliva turns starch into sugar.

teach.heading: Lock and key
bullets: Each enzyme has an active site
teach.note: Use a jigsaw image. Body temperature (37 °C) is ideal for most human enzymes.

teach.heading: Investigating amylase
bullets: Test drops with iodine every minute
When iodine stays orange, starch has gone
teach.note: Show the demo video. Model reading results.

model.problem: Iodine stays blue-black for 4 minutes at 20 °C but only 1 minute at 37 °C. Explain.
steps: Starch is broken down faster at 37 °C
Amylase works fastest near body temperature
More collisions and enzyme is not denatured

misconception.right: High temperature denatures enzymes: the active site changes shape

check.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids; protease breaks them apart.

independent: Core: Complete an enzyme table: enzyme, substrate, product, location
Extend: Explain why stomach protease works best at a low pH but amylase in the mouth does not
Stretch: Plan the amylase–temperature investigation: variables, method, risk assessment and predicted graph.
exit: What is an enzyme?
Products of lipase?
Why does bread taste sweeter when chewed?
lessons.homework: Chew a small piece of plain bread for two minutes and describe the taste change, explaining it with the word amylase.
lessons.send: Support: lock-and-key diagram. Stretch: optimum pH graphs.

lessons.title: Absorption and the small intestine

Explain how villi are adapted for absorption
Describe the role of bacteria in the gut

lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the careful design of the body

keywords.def: small food molecules passing into the blood
finger-like projections lining the small intestine
the total area of the outside of something
particles spreading from high to low concentration

starter: Why must molecules be small to be absorbed?
Surface area of a 1 cm cube?

teach.heading: From gut to blood
bullets: Small molecules diffuse into the blood
Cells use them for energy and growth

teach.heading: Villi: built for absorption
teach.note: Answer the big question. The small intestine's surface area is often compared to a tennis court.

model.problem: Explain how villi are adapted for absorption (3 marks)
steps: Millions of villi give a large surface area, so more absorption at once
Thin walls give a short distance for diffusion
A good blood supply carries molecules away, keeping the concentration gradient
model.answer: Area + thin + blood supply, each linked to faster absorption

teach.heading: Helpful bacteria
teach.note: Antibiotics can kill useful gut bacteria too.

misconception.wrong: Food is absorbed in the stomach
misconception.right: Most absorption of nutrients happens in the small intestine

check.q: Why are villi walls only one cell thick?
options: To give a short diffusion distance
check.why: A thin wall means molecules diffuse a short distance into the blood, so absorption is faster.

independent: Core: Draw and label a villus with three adaptations explained
Extend: Coeliac disease damages villi. Predict and explain the effects on a person
Stretch: Model surface area: compare a 4 cm cube with eight 2 cm cubes. Link your answer to villi.
exit: What does absorption mean?
Give two adaptations of villi.
Name one job of gut bacteria.
lessons.homework: Make a model of a villus from household items (photo to upload) and label its adaptations.
lessons.send: Support: diagram with labels. Stretch: coeliac case study.

lessons.title: Burning fuels

objectives: Describe combustion as a reaction with oxygen

Test for carbon dioxide and water
successCriteria: Write a word equation for burning methane
Describe tests for carbon dioxide and water
Explain why mass seems to disappear when a fuel burns

lessons.smsc: Cultural: the role of oil in Gulf economies; moral: responsible energy use

keywords.def: burning: a reaction with oxygen that releases energy
a substance that releases energy when burnt
a compound of hydrogen and carbon only
turns milky with carbon dioxide
releases energy to the surroundings

starter: Name the gas we need for respiration
Name a fuel used at home
What happens to a candle as it burns?

teach.heading: Fuel + oxygen
bullets: Hydrocarbons make carbon dioxide and water

model.problem: Write a word equation for burning methane
steps: Reactants: methane + oxygen
Products of a hydrocarbon: carbon dioxide + water
methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

teach.heading: Testing the products
bullets: Water: blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink (or anhydrous copper sulfate turns blue)

teach.note: Answer the big question: oxygen from the air is added, so the products weigh more than the wax that burnt.

misconception.right: Atoms are rearranged into gases; mass is conserved

check.q: A gas turns limewater milky. It is…
check.why: Limewater is the test for carbon dioxide. Water is tested with cobalt chloride or copper sulfate.

practice: Name the two products of burning a hydrocarbon

Stretch: Design an experiment to show that the products of a burning candle weigh more than the wax used.

Test for carbon dioxide?
Products of burning methane?

a compound of an element with oxygen

put out a fire

keywords.def: gases trapping heat in the atmosphere, warming the Earth
a gas that traps heat, e.g. carbon dioxide, methane
the rise in Earth's average temperature
long-term changes in weather patterns

starter: What percentage of air is oxygen (roughly)?

teach.heading: The greenhouse effect
bullets: More greenhouse gases trap more heat
teach.note: Without it, Earth's average would be about −18 °C instead of about 15 °C.
cycle: Earth warms and gives off heat

teach.heading: Rising carbon dioxide
teach.note: Answer the big question: tiny amounts still absorb lots of heat energy. Show the Keeling curve.

teach.heading: Correlation and cause
bullets: Temperature and CO₂ have risen together
Scientists have tested the cause carefully
teach.note: The scientific consensus is that human activity is the main cause of recent warming.

misconception.wrong: The greenhouse effect is the same as the ozone hole
misconception.right: They are different problems: the ozone layer protects from UV light

teach.heading: Responses
bullets: Insulate homes, travel less by car
teach.note: Link to the Islamic principle of moderation and avoiding waste (israf).

check.q: How do greenhouse gases warm the Earth?
options: They absorb heat given off by the Earth and re-radiate it
They make holes in the ozone layer
check.why: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared from Earth's surface and send some back. C is a different problem.

practice: Describe the greenhouse effect in three steps
Give one effect of climate change
independent: Core: Use the CO₂ table to describe the trend and suggest a reason
Extend: Evaluate three ways a family could reduce its carbon footprint
Stretch: Explain why some scientists say methane is a bigger short-term problem than CO₂, even though there is less of it.
exit: What is global warming?
Main source of extra CO₂?
One thing you could do to reduce emissions?
lessons.homework: Calculate your family's approximate carbon footprint with an online calculator and choose two realistic changes.
lessons.send: Support: diagram with labels. Stretch: feedback loops (ice melting).

lessons.title: Fuels for the future
lessons.bigQuestion: What should power the world when fossil fuels run out?
objectives: Compare fossil fuels and alternatives
Describe hydrogen as a fuel
Evaluate fuels using evidence
successCriteria: List advantages and disadvantages of fossil fuels
Explain why hydrogen burns cleanly
Evaluate a fuel choice using several criteria
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: energy resources; Business: energy costs
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness to future generations and to poorer countries

keywords.def: a fuel formed from ancient living things: coal, oil, gas
will run out; cannot be replaced
a fuel made from plants or animal waste
burns to make only water

teach.heading: Fossil fuels
teach.note: Recap and link to the last lesson.

teach.heading: Hydrogen
bullets: No carbon dioxide at the point of use
Hard to store; often made using fossil fuels
teach.note: Show the 'squeaky pop' test video for hydrogen.

left.title: Hydrogen
points: Renewable if made with solar power

model.problem: Evaluate biofuel (ethanol from sugar cane) for cars
steps: Advantage: renewable; plants absorb CO₂ as they grow
Disadvantage: needs farmland that could grow food
Disadvantage: still releases CO₂ when burnt
Judgement: useful in some countries, but not the full answer

teach.heading: Carbon neutral?
teach.note: Farming and transport also release CO₂.

misconception.right: They release CO₂ when burnt, partly balanced by plant growth

check.q: What is the only product when hydrogen burns in oxygen?
check.why: Hydrogen contains no carbon, so only water (H₂O) forms.

independent: Core: Complete a table comparing coal, natural gas, hydrogen and biofuel
Extend: Write a reasoned recommendation for a fuel for city buses
Stretch: Explain why hydrogen made by electrolysis using electricity from coal is not truly 'clean'.
exit: Why are fossil fuels non-renewable?
Product of burning hydrogen?
One disadvantage of biofuels?
lessons.homework: Research one country's plan to reduce fossil fuel use and summarise it in a paragraph.
lessons.send: Support: comparison table frame. Stretch: energy density data.

lessons.title: 8E review: combustion
lessons.bigQuestion: What is the most important thing everyone should know about combustion?
objectives: Retrieve key knowledge from 8E
Apply it to unfamiliar situations
Improve answers using feedback
successCriteria: Recall equations, tests and the fire triangle
Answer data and safety questions
Write a 6-mark evaluation

keywords.def: gaining oxygen
burning with too little oxygen
rain made acidic by pollutants
trapping of heat by gases

starter: Three sides of the fire triangle?

model.problem: Evaluate replacing gas boilers with electric heat pumps (6 marks)
steps: For: no combustion at home, so no CO risk
For: lower CO₂ if electricity is renewable
Against: expensive to install
Against: if electricity comes from fossil fuels, CO₂ is still released
Conclusion: best long-term option as the grid becomes renewable

misconception.right: CO has no smell; gas companies add a smell to natural gas, not to CO

check.q: A Bunsen burner has a yellow flame and blackens a beaker. Why?
check.why: Yellow flame and soot show incomplete combustion. Opening the air hole adds oxygen.

practice: Word equations for complete and incomplete burning of methane
independent: Core: 8E end-of-unit check (school 8E assessment pack)
Extend: 6-mark evaluation of hydrogen-powered cars
Stretch: Interpret CO₂ and temperature data from 1960 to today and evaluate the evidence for human-caused warming.
exit: My strongest 8E topic
My weakest 8E topic
One action I'll take for the environment
lessons.homework: Revise 8E and complete DIRT corrections on your end-of-unit check.
lessons.send: Support: knowledge organiser. Stretch: data evaluation.
